sources.title: We Just Had The First Humanoid Robot Strike Ever
Hyundai workers in South Korea strike over humanoids
Hyundai Workers Walk Out in Auto Industry's First Humanoid Robot Strike
How Hyundai's humanoid robot plans are facing fierce opposition from workers (video, KOREA NOW)

chunks.text: About 35,000 workers at Hyundai's car [[plants]] in South Korea {{walked out}} in July over a plan to put [[humanoid]] robots on the factory floor. Their [[union]] says no car company anywhere has faced a [[strike]] about robots before. The workers are not asking Hyundai to {{call off}} the plan. They want the right to agree before any robot arrives.

verbs.correct: To stop work as a protest

verbs.wrong: To delay a plan to a later year

chunks.text: Hyundai owns Boston Dynamics, an American robot maker, and intends to install about 25,000 of its Atlas robots at Hyundai and Kia plants worldwide. The first are due at a factory in Savannah, in the United States, starting in 2028. No date has been fixed for South Korea. The Korean Metal Workers' Union is {{holding out for}} a written promise that no humanoid robot enters a Korean plant unless the union agrees first. It is also {{pushing for}} [[hourly]] jobs to be {{turned into}} fixed [[salaries]], and for the [[retirement age]] to rise from 60 to 65.

verbs.wrong: To wait without making any demands
To vote in favor of an agreement
To be paid at a higher hourly rate

chunks.text: The action {{built up}} slowly. Between July 13 and 15 the workers left their [[shifts]] two hours early. On July 20 they moved to four hour [[stoppages]] every day at the Ulsan [[complex]], which is the largest car factory in the world. Those first three days alone stopped about 5,000 cars from being built. Hyundai will not promise that [[automation]] costs no jobs. It says workers will {{move into}} [[supervising]] and repairing the machines instead. Managers have {{put forward}} higher pay, large [[bonuses]] and 15 company [[shares]] for each worker.

verbs.wrong: To start again after a break

verbs.correct: To change to a new role
verbs.wrong: To be trained for a short period
To pay something before it is due

chunks.text: Neither side has {{backed down}}. What is [[settled]] in Ulsan matters well [[beyond]] South Korea, because other [[carmakers]] are testing the same machines and are watching how this {{works out}}. The union's argument is not that robots cannot do the job. It is that the people doing the job now were never asked first.

verbs.wrong: To refuse to speak to the other side
To be decided by a judge

mainIdea.s: About 35,000 Hyundai workers in South Korea walked out over a plan to bring in humanoid robots. They are not trying to stop the robots, but want the right to agree before any robot arrives.
mainIdea.why: The union said no automaker had ever faced a robot strike before. It is not against the robots, it wants a say before any robot enters a Korean plant.

mainIdea.s: Tens of thousands of Hyundai workers stopped work in South Korea, demanding the company scrap its robot plan. Managers offered higher pay and bonuses, but the union has not backed down.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the union never asked Hyundai to cancel the robot plan. It only wants the right to agree before any robot arrives at a plant.

mainIdea.s: Boston Dynamics showed off a new version of its Atlas robot at an event in Massachusetts last year. The update focused on warehouse tasks and faster movement, not work inside car plants.
mainIdea.why: This is about an earlier robot unveiling, not the 2026 strike at Hyundai's Korean plants. Boston Dynamics is mentioned only as the maker of the robots Hyundai plans to use.
